chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

that Amir al-Mu'minin (blessings of God upon him) said: 'Verily, among the visitors of the sick with the greatest recompense in the presence of God, Mighty and Majestic, is the one who, when he visits his brother, shortens the sitting — unless the patient happens to love that and wants it and requests it from him.'
And he (peace be upon him) said: 'Part of the completion of visiting the sick is that the visitor places one of his hands upon the other or upon his forehead.'

key_terms.الجبهة: Forehead — placing a hand on the patient's forehead is a traditional gesture of sympathy and blessing
key_terms.العُوَّاد: Plural of 'a'id — those who visit the sick (عيادة المريض, visiting the sick, is a recommended act in Islamic law)
key_terms.تمام العيادة: The completion/perfection of the visit — what makes the visit fully proper and meritorious
key_terms.خفَّف الجلوس: To lighten the sitting — i.e., to shorten one's stay at the patient's bedside

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali say about the etiquette and duration of visiting the sick?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS), as transmitted through Imam al-Sadiq (AS), gives two practical guidelines for visiting the sick: first, that the best visits are brief unless the patient wishes for a longer stay; and second, that placing one's hand over the other or on the patient's forehead is an act that completes the visit. This teaching reflects the Islamic ethical framework around caring for the ill — the visitor should prioritize the patient's comfort and wellbeing rather than their own social inclinations. The practice of placing hands on the patient's forehead echoes traditional gestures of care, sympathy, and blessings.
